spoiler_text: #Reading in Week Ten of 2026 | Mar 02‒08 | ~2100 words | ~12k characters | Tag to mute: #BokBooks
content:
●●●●○ Dobridust - Margaret St. Clair (ss) 1948¹
Jick worked at the UN Spaceport, and was given to smuggling out "gifts" for his wife Oona, which concerned her, since she'd read of one man who got sentenced to three years on Pluto for doing the same.

This time Jick had snuck out a Dobridust, an automated wall-cleaning device, like an ever-running robot vacuum. It worried Oona that it was stamped "Property of UN Spaceport" all over. What if a United Nations Bureau of Investigation agent showed up one day? Jick assured her that would never happen. Then one day it did, only a half-hour before the other wives were due to show up for the Maroola club meeting. Oona panicked, and accidentally knocked out the agent. So she had to hide the unconscious man, then the ladies arrived, and… A comedy of errors.

●●●◐○ Lydia's Private Casket - James Gault (ss) 2021
It's 1934, and seventeen-year-old Lydia is spending a summer at a naturist resort in Czechoslovakia, where she meets Franz, the son of a man her father had gone to school with, and with whom her family is vacationing. Both plan to go into medicine, and many letters are exchanged in later years.

It's April 1940, and Lydia is working as a new doctor, treating wounded soldiers at a British military hospital, when a major in Intelligence comes to ask why she's received a letter from Luxembourg, an occupied country. She goes away with him.

It's 1980 and Lydia — the great-niece of the original — is called to the Ministry of Defense. She receives a casket (a small chest, as for jewelry) of letters that shows what happened to the original Lydia, who didn't die when her hospital was bombed in the Blitz, as her mother believed.

●●●○○ Ill Wind - Doug Beason, Kevin J. Anderson (nov) 1996
A disaster novel with a cast of thousands. Well, dozens. A supertanker crashed into Golden Bate Bridge, spilling almost a million gallons of oil. In the uproar that followed, OilStar, the company that owned the oil and ship, got permission to release an incompletely tested oil-eating bacteria.

It was very effective. It was frighteningly effective, since its designer had lost his son in the latest oil war, and his wife and daughter in a car accident. His life would have been much better without oil, so he tweaked the bacteria and faked the data. It spread like wildfire, eating oil, gasoline, plastic, and much more. This is the story of how US civilization coped. (It spread to other countries, but this book ignores that.)

We have the Wyoming-cowboy fixer for the oil company, who'd been in the copter spreading the oil. The ruthless oil company president, the scientist, the PR people. The House Speaker who ended up president when POTUS and the VP were killed, who proved spectacularly bad for the job. The general who imposed martial law on Albuquerque, ham-handedly. The solar scientist with a plan.³ A couple of dozen characters, some of whom lived, and many who died.

●●●◐○ The Moon Is Green - Fritz Leiber (ss) 1952
Effie and her husband lived in an underground silo after the Big War. Hank had gotten a promotion, and as a Council member now, they'd moved to the top floor, which was above ground level.² The flat even had windows, with interior lead shutters.

Effie — who felt horribly repressed by underground living, and who was a trial to her status-conscious husband — had several times opened those shutters to gaze out at the surface world, and been yelled at by Hank, and had to be "counted" using a Geiger counter afterward. One day a man showed up outside the window…

●●○○○ The Big Eye - Max Ehrlich (nov) 1949
The intensity dial for the Cold War had swung around so far it was about to go into Hot. The Soviet Union occupied Europe and much of Asia, and it looked like it had a secret weapon that was causing problems with stratocruisers — and also earthquakes. America's big cities had been evacuated, since they were natural targets of the big bombs. The president and the military were to hold a meeting tomorrow to decide if war was inevitable, and whether to attack first.

Dr. Dawson of Palomar Observatory phoned the president with good news: The Soviets didn't have a secret weapon. The next day he and twenty of the world's top astronomers delivered the bad news: the earthquakes and other problems were caused by the gravity of a rogue planet approaching our world.⁴ In twenty-five months it would collide with Earth, on Christmas Day, 1962. Might as well call off World War III.

The effects were immediate. Waves of suicides, crowded asylums, people drinking themselves to death, riots. But they were also positive: governments found out they could provide food, shelter, and health care for all who needed it. Poverty began to disappear. A World Federation was formed.

The book suffers from a lack of scientific knowledge, particularly orbital mechanics. The rogue planet is called the Big Eye: “the black eyebrow was a huge, curved volcanic mountain range, that the eyeball was a great round crater, that the iris was a darker depression within the crater,” while the other side of the frozen planet was plain. The intruder also has a rotation period of eight months. Yet the story had the the disk visible for too long and the face appear unchanging in the sky for too long.

It also suffers because it's very of its time. For example, when it notes that violence went down, it says “Not a Jew was murdered, not a Negro lynched.” Loads of little comments made in passing just grate.

●●●●○ Of What We Never Were - David Robertson (ss) 2025
Adam's parents and sister died in a car accident. Twelve-year-old Adam was taken to a hospital, but the prognosis was terminal. His grandparents agreed to let his body be used for a whole-brain emulation process. With her mother's permission, his best friend Stacy was roped in to test the sim made from scanning Adam's brain, with Stacy getting a special tablet that let her and Adam 2.0 text to each other.

Stacy copes with the death of her friend, who's somehow still alive within her tablet, with her teacher and school counselor being the only other adults who knew Stacy could communicate with the new Adam. The experiment went well from Stacy and the researchers' points of view, less so from that of the school authorities.

●●●○○ The Wines of Earth - Margaret St. Clair (ss) 1957
Widower Joe ran his small winery in California. One day while walking his vineyard in the off season to see if the rain had damaged the terraces, he encountered four odd young people. They claimed to be making a tour of the nearer galaxy, and were spending their few hours on Earth at his winery. Joe offered them some wine, then they invited him into their ship and offered him some of theirs.

●●○○○ A Defiant Departure - MacSmart Ojiludu (ss) 2021
Indra lost her first child to a miscarriage. She lost her second to an infant infection. She and Chika had remained married, but the feeling was gone. Her third child — "the baby" — was alive, but Indra refused to become emotionally attached until the boy was at least three years old, and didn't even think of him by name.

In climate-change Nigeria, there was sometimes drought, but more often flood, and the Niger was rising again, but Chika said they were safe. Until on one outing in the knee-high waters, Chika saw a crocodile attack a neighbor. He panicked, and told Indra to evacuate with him. The baby slowed her down, and Chika waded ahead. He was lost to the waters, then Indra and the baby followed. All drowned. Indra's last thoughts were about the rescue crews who'd have to recover and identify the bodies of her and all her neighbors.

You want a collection to confuse and depress you? I recommend Disruption, edited by Rachel Zadok et al. Six more stories to endure.

●●◐○○ Emergency Call - E C Tubb (ss) 1956
This story was designed to provide a problem. A spaceship is on a cargo run from Earth to Mars. It's constructed as a long central corridor with spheres strung along it: navigation and living, cargo, life support, fuel, engine. Thus a small meteorite can blow up the life support sphere without killing anyone.

This means the ship must get to Mars faster, before their emergency air stores run out. That means unloading all the cargo — which in pre-cargo-container times meant throwing boxes out by hand — and then increasing speed. Except the engines can only be run for twenty minutes at a time, then they have to cool down for hours (we get a lecture about conduction, convection, and radiation, and how only the last works in space, slowly).

Oh, and something else you might not know: cosmic rays cause aging. One Earth's surface, under miles of atmosphere, aging is slow. “Deep sea creatures protected by a mile of water don’t suffer from old age.” And in space, people age quickly, and a twenty-year-old spacer is dead by fifty.

So this is the tale of what the four spacers do to save themselves, and at what cost.

●●●◐○ House Hunting - Mel Cowan (ss) 2025
Going by this author, long-time nudists do nothing interesting, so all stories have to be about new people coming to nudism. In this case, thirtyish Ellie had been downsized six months ago, and her redundancy package was almost gone, so she had to give up her apartment and find shared accommodation. Nothing she saw was affordable, until she widened her search criteria and found a promising place for an "open-minded individual".

When she went to the old house to look, she was greeted by a nude man. The house was shared by four nudists: three thirty-something creatives and a retired teacher. They didn't demand Ellie become a nudist, but she had to be chill with them remaining unclothed. The place was her best option, so Ellie agreed.

So the story is how Ellie came to cope with the nudity, and went from hiding from it to accepting it, and when a heat wave struck, finally trying it herself, and coming to like it.

●●●◐○ Tethered {Middle Falls Ghosts 01} - Shawn Inmon (nvt) 2023
The Middle Falls stories are about a person dying and being recycled to an earlier point in their lives to try again. But apparently another option is becoming a ghost. Lucy had been a maid who'd died in 1977 at age 17. (Yes, this sounds odd; it's dealt with.) She was now stuck within Stafford Mansion, along with Frederick, who'd been lord of the manor a century before, and who'd almost faded away, as apparently ghosts do.

One day widowed Christine bought the run-down old place cheap and moved in. She was accompanied by her two kids: eight-year-old daughter Frankie (who was able to see Lucy almost from the start), and fifteen-year-old son Eddie (who managed to see Lucy after a few weeks). The kids help Lucy find out why she's trapped, and help her move on.

━━━━━━━━━━

[1] The things that get mentioned in stories, that are background details unrelated to the plot. “They stayed at the Hotel Brahe, on the slopes of Mt. Tycho, and even made a couple of trips to the dark side and brought back chunks of fossilized edelweiss for souvenirs.” Fossilized flowers on Luna, and it means nothing.

[2] This strikes me as the worst floor to live on, post apocalypse.

[3] A very dated one, since he held that solar power satellites beaming microwaves to receiving arrays on Earth was obviously cheaper and easier than using ground-based photovoltaics.

[4] No way are the gravitational effects noticeable before the planet is readily observable to anyone looking up at night. But Erlich wasn't an SF writer: his novels were thrillers, and he also wrote a lot for radio, film, and television.

content:
The #wildfire situation in Halifax is a good reminder that you should have and maintain a go bag so that if you have to leave home in a moment’s notice you’re ready. Additionally, keep critical documents and medicine in an easy to reach location.

Being prepared now will save lives later.

Fires, flooding, earthquakes, hurricanes, and many man-made hazards are some of the reasons why you may need to #evacuate.

#BePrepared

https://www.readyforwildfire.org/prepare-for-wildfire/get-set/emergency-supply-kit/
